headline: A virus, a brain scan and a penguin: what can one number hide?
teaser: Is a lost label only a symbol? Would you want to know your future risk? Can an average hide a collapse?

articles.title: A Symbolic Loss? The US Loses Its Measles Elimination Status
articles.dek: After 26 years, measles is again spreading continuously in the United States. Is a lost label only a symbol, or a warning about how communities protect one another?
paras: For more than a quarter of a century, the United States could claim that measles no longer lived within its borders. In 2000, health authorities declared the disease "eliminated," meaning that although travellers still occasionally brought the virus in from abroad, it no longer spread continuously inside the country. This month, that claim appears to have collapsed. According to multiple news reports, a regional commission of the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), which met from November 10 to 13, concluded that measles has circulated in the US without interruption for more than a year. A formal announcement is expected shortly, but the verdict is already being described as a turning point for American public health.

The rule behind the decision is simple. A country loses its elimination status when a single chain of measles transmission continues for 12 months or longer. In this case, scientists did not have to rely on guesswork. By sequencing 1,760 virus samples collected across North America, researchers showed that they belonged to one expanding lineage, which indicates that the infections were connected rather than the result of separate imports. An outbreak in Utah, which passed the one-year mark in June, proved decisive.

The numbers explain why experts are alarmed. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has confirmed 5,412 cases in 2026 as of November 12, more than double the 2,289 recorded in 2025 and the highest annual total since 1991. State health departments have reported 10 measles-related deaths this year, although the CDC's own count is six, partly because officials classify some deaths differently. Measles is one of the most contagious diseases known: a single infected person can pass it to most of the unprotected people around them, and the virus can linger in the air of a room for up to two hours after that person has left.

Because the virus spreads so easily, controlling it depends on what scientists call herd immunity. When roughly 95 percent of a population is immune, an imported case usually fizzles out, because the virus cannot find enough susceptible people to keep spreading. Below that level, outbreaks can grow and persist. In the United States, the share of kindergarten children who have received both recommended doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine has fallen from 95.2 percent in the 2019–2020 school year to 92.4 percent in 2025–2026. A drop of fewer than three percentage points may sound minor, yet nationwide it represents many thousands of additional unprotected children every year, and they are often concentrated in particular communities, where coverage can be far lower.

Why has coverage slipped? Researchers point to several overlapping causes. The COVID-19 pandemic interrupted routine medical check-ups, misleading claims about vaccine safety have spread widely online, and more families have used exemptions that allow children to attend school without the usual vaccines. Some public-health experts also argue that mixed messages from political leaders, including Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has publicly questioned the safety of some vaccines, have weakened trust. His supporters counter that parents deserve more information and greater freedom to make medical decisions for their own children.

Not everyone agrees that the lost status itself matters very much. PAHO imposes no sanctions or travel restrictions on countries that lose it, and some commentators describe the change as largely symbolic: the virus does not care about labels, and the outbreaks were already happening. Others insist that the symbol carries real weight. Elimination status, they argue, works like a report card, and losing it signals that the country's defences, from vaccination rates to disease surveillance, are no longer strong enough. A recent letter in the medical journal The Lancet found that the US failed four of seven CDC indicators used to monitor elimination.

Regaining the title will not be quick. The country would need to go at least 12 months without sustained transmission, and simply ending today's outbreaks would not be enough if coverage keeps falling, since every new imported case would carry a higher risk of igniting another long chain. Other countries offer both hope and warning. Venezuela lost its status in 2018 and recovered it in 2023, and Brazil, which lost it in 2019, regained it in November 2024. Canada, however, which lost its status about a year ago, is still classified as having endemic measles.

In the end, the episode raises a question that reaches beyond one disease: how should a society balance individual choice against collective protection? Vaccination is a personal medical decision, but its benefits are shared, because immune people also shield infants too young to be vaccinated and patients whose immune systems are weak. Whether the US restores its status may depend less on new science than on whether that shared logic can persuade enough families.

speak.p: Some people think that the government should make important health decisions for the public, such as requiring vaccines. Others think individuals should make these decisions for themselves. Which view do you agree with, and why? Use specific reasons and examples.
speak.hint: State your view → reason 1 (protecting others / personal freedom) + example → reason 2 + example → short conclusion.

write.p: Professor: This week, health authorities reportedly concluded that measles has been spreading continuously in the United States for more than a year, ending the country's "elimination" status after 26 years. Vaccination coverage among young children has slipped from about 95 to 92 percent. Some people argue that schools should require vaccines for all students unless there is a medical reason. Others believe parents should be free to decide. What do you think: should schools be allowed to require vaccinations for students? Why or why not? (Mia says: Yes. Measles is extremely contagious, and some children cannot be vaccinated because they are ill. When schools require vaccines, they protect the most vulnerable students. A school is a shared space, so the rules should protect everyone.) (Daniel says: I am not sure that strict rules are the best answer. If parents feel forced, they may trust doctors even less. I think schools should focus on education and make vaccines easy to get, while still respecting families' choices.)
steps: Decide your position: require vaccines, or encourage them without forcing.
Give one reason, such as protecting classmates who cannot be vaccinated.
Respond to Mia or Daniel: agree with one point and challenge another.
End with a clear one-sentence conclusion.

articles.title: Is It Better to Know? A Brain Scan That Predicts Alzheimer's Years Early
articles.dek: A simple resting brain scan may reveal Alzheimer's risk long before symptoms appear. But if there is no cure, is early knowledge a gift or a burden?
paras: Alzheimer's disease usually announces itself slowly: a forgotten appointment, a repeated question, a familiar route that suddenly feels confusing. By the time such symptoms appear, however, the brain has often been changing for a decade or more. A new study from Stanford Medicine, published in the journal Science Advances, suggests that some of those hidden changes can be detected years earlier, using nothing more than a brain scan taken while a person lies quietly and rests.

The researchers used a technique called resting-state functional MRI, which tracks how different regions of the brain become active together even when a person is not performing any task. These patterns of coordination form a kind of map of the brain's communication network, often called the connectome. The team, led by senior author Yu Zhang, compared the connectomes of 180 so-called "super agers," older adults whose memory remains unusually sharp, with those of 110 people who had already been diagnosed with Alzheimer's disease. From the differences, they built a single number: the Alzheimer's resilience-vulnerability connectome score, or ARC.

The score separated the two groups with about 85 percent accuracy. More importantly, the researchers then tested it on more than 1,300 adults aged 55 to 70 who showed no signs of memory problems at all, drawing on data from several long-running research projects. Over follow-up periods of up to 12 years, people whose brains looked more "Alzheimer's-like" were more likely to experience faster cognitive decline, to accumulate amyloid-beta, a sticky protein strongly associated with the disease, and eventually to receive a diagnosis. According to the authors, ARC performed as well as, or better than, established biomarkers, and its predictions improved further when it was combined with them.

Supporters of early detection see obvious benefits. Scientists designing prevention trials struggle to find volunteers who will actually develop the disease, and a reliable score could help them select the right participants and measure whether an intervention works. Individuals, too, might gain time to plan their finances, discuss future care with their families, or adopt habits linked to healthier ageing, such as regular exercise. Furthermore, recently approved drugs that clear amyloid from the brain appear to work best, modestly slowing decline, when they are given at an early stage.

Yet a prediction is not a diagnosis, and the authors themselves stress that ARC is not intended to diagnose Alzheimer's. An accuracy of 85 percent sounds impressive, but it also means that a meaningful number of people could be misclassified. Some might be told they face a high risk and spend years worrying about an illness that never arrives, while others might be falsely reassured. Because there is still no cure, critics ask what a person should actually do with the knowledge that their brain resembles that of someone with dementia.

There are also concerns that reach beyond the clinic. Brain-scan data are deeply personal, and ethicists warn that predictive scores could one day be misused, for example by insurers or employers, if laws do not protect them. Access raises another issue: MRI scans are expensive, so such tests might be available mainly to wealthier patients, and the people studied so far may not represent every population. Finally, a single number risks making the future seem fixed, even though the researchers note that scores can change over time.

That possibility of change is precisely what the team plans to explore next. They intend to run a trial testing whether cognitive training can shift a person's ARC score toward the healthier pattern seen in super agers. If it can, the scan could become more than a warning; it could become a way to track whether prevention efforts are working. If it cannot, doubts about the value of early knowledge are likely to grow stronger.

For now, the study is best understood as a promising research tool rather than a test that anyone can request from their doctor. It nonetheless raises a difficult question that medicine will face more and more often as prediction improves: is it always better to know?

articles.title: Schrödinger's Penguin: One Species, Two Opposite Fates
articles.dek: One population of erect-crested penguins is stable while the other is collapsing. Should conservation rules judge a species by its average or by its weakest part?
paras: In a famous thought experiment, the physicist Erwin Schrödinger imagined a cat that is, in a sense, both alive and dead until someone opens the box. A team of penguin researchers has borrowed the idea to describe a strange conservation puzzle. Their study, published in the journal PLOS ONE, concerns the erect-crested penguin, a striking bird with a spiky golden crest, and it suggests that the species is simultaneously doing quite well and heading for trouble, depending on where you look.

Erect-crested penguins breed in only two places on Earth, both remote island groups in the Southern Ocean south-east of New Zealand. The Bounty Islands are tiny, covering roughly 50 hectares of bare rock, while the Antipodes Islands are about 40 times larger. Because the islands are so hard to reach, the birds have rarely been surveyed, and the species' official "Endangered" listing still relies heavily on estimates from 1978, which suggested about 115,000 breeding pairs on each island group and which scientists now consider unreliable.

To produce better numbers, the team, led by Thomas Mattern of the Global Penguin Society and the University of Otago, used drones to photograph the colonies between 2022 and 2024. They counted roughly 27,800 breeding pairs on the Bounty Islands and about 29,800 on the Antipodes, giving a total of around 57,600 pairs. On the surface, the two populations look almost identical in size. Their histories, however, are completely different. The Bounty population appears to have been stable for at least 25 years, whereas the Antipodes population has fallen by more than 40 percent since the mid-1990s, an average decline of about 1.5 percent per year.

What explains such different fates for birds of the same species? One answer lies with a predator. The Antipodes are home to resident subantarctic skuas, large seabirds that hunt penguin chicks. As colonies there shrink and break into smaller, scattered groups, the adults become less able to defend their young collectively, so more chicks are lost and the colonies shrink further. Ecologists call this self-reinforcing pattern an Allee effect. The Bounty Islands, by contrast, have no resident skuas. The researchers also note differences at sea: after breeding, Antipodes birds travel south and east, while Bounty birds tend to stay closer to home, so the two groups may experience different ocean conditions and food supplies.

The real paradox emerges when conservation officials try to assign the species a single threat category. If the two populations are simply combined, the overall picture could support moving the species down from "Endangered" to the less serious category of "Vulnerable." On paper, that would look like good news. The authors argue that it would actually be misleading, because an average would conceal the collapse taking place on the Antipodes. Assessed separately, they suggest, the Antipodes population would still deserve to be listed as Endangered, and even the stable Bounty population might qualify as Vulnerable, simply because its entire range is confined to one very small archipelago where a single disaster could be devastating.

The debate is not merely academic. Threat categories influence how governments spend money and write regulations. The researchers worry that a global downlisting could be used to justify weakening protections around the Bounty Islands, where fishing restrictions are already limited: more than 40 percent of the surrounding territorial sea is excluded from protection to allow a longline fishery for a fish called ling. In their view, the Bounty colonies may be the species' last stable stronghold, which makes protecting them more urgent, not less.

Some might reasonably reply that classification systems need simple, consistent rules, and that assessing every population separately would demand data that do not exist for most species. Fishing communities, too, depend on access to productive waters, and their livelihoods also deserve consideration. Still, the erect-crested penguin shows how a single number can hide important differences. The lesson applies far beyond penguins: before trusting an average, it is worth asking what it might be averaging away.
